etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English sand, from Old English sand, from Proto-West Germanic *samd, from Proto-Germanic *samdaz, from Proto-Indo-European *sámh₂dʰos, from *sem- (“to pour”).

See also West Frisian sân, Dutch zand, German Sand, Danish, Swedish and Norwegian sand, Latin sabulum, Ancient Greek ἄμαθος (ámathos), English dialectal samel (“sand bottom”), Old Irish do·essim (“to pour out”), Latin sentina (“bilge water”), Lithuanian sémti (“to scoop”), Ancient Greek ἀμάω (amáō, “to gather”), ἄμη (ámē, “water bucket”).

definitions.definition: (countable) A specific grade, type, or composition of sand.

quote.text: One sand was that used in cement testing with white well rounded smooth grains, passing through a 20-mesh sieve and retained on a 30-mesh sieve. The other was ordinary brown building sand, passing 40-mesh and retained on 60-mesh.

definitions.definition: (countable, often in the plural) A beach or other mass of sand.

quote.citation: 1892, James Yoxall, chapter 14, in The Lonely Pyramid:
quote.text: From east and south the danger was to be expected. Not from the uninhabited northern desert, not from the desolate sands of the unknown west, would it come.

definitions.definition: (uncountable) Rock that is ground more finely than gravel, but is not as fine as silt (more formally, see grain sizes chart), forming beaches and deserts and also used in construction.

quote.citation: 1913, Joseph C[rosby] Lincoln, chapter I, in Mr. Pratt’s Patients, New York, N.Y., London: D[aniel] Appleton and Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: For a spell we done pretty well. Then there came a reg'lar terror of a sou'wester same as you don't get one summer in a thousand, and blowed the shanty flat and ripped about half of the weir poles out of the sand.

quote.citation: 2018, Neil Tweedie, “Is the world running out of sand? The truth behind stolen beaches and dredged islands”, in The Guardian‎[1]:
quote.text: “We are addicted to sand but don’t know it because we don’t buy it as individuals,” says Aurora Torres,  […]

quote.citation: 2018, Neil Tweedie, “Is the world running out of sand? The truth behind stolen beaches and dredged islands”, in The Guardian‎[2]:
quote.text: China’s hunger for sand is insatiable, its biggest dredging site at Lake Poyang produces 989,000 tonnes per day.

quote.citation: 1884, Mark Twain, The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn:
quote.text: You may say what you want to, but in my opinion she had more sand in her than any girl I ever see; in my opinion she was just full of sand.
He said, “I admire your sand but I believe you will find I am not liable for such claims. Let me say too that your valuation of the horse is high by about two hundred dollars.”
There was youngsters all around him, and he stood there lookin’ at me and never turned a hair. He had sand, that Morrell.

definitions.definition: (uncountable, geology) A particle from 62.5 microns to 2 mm in diameter, following the Wentworth scale.
A light beige colour, like that of typical sand.
(countable, obsolete) A single grain of sand.

quote.citation: 1611 April (first recorded performance), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Cymbeline”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene v]:
quote.text: One sand another. Not more resembles that sweet rosy lad

definitions.definition: (countable, figurative) A moment or interval of time; the term or extent of one's life (referring to the sand in an hourglass).

quote.citation: c. 1591–1592 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Third Part of Henry the Sixt, […]”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene iv]:
quote.text: The sands are numbered that make up my life.

quote.citation: 1838 October, Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, “A Psalm of Life. […]”, in Voices of the Night, Cambridge, Mass.:  […]  John Owen, published 1839, →OCLC, stanza 7, page 7:
quote.text: […]  And, departing, leave behind us / Footprints on the sands of time  […]

definitions.definition: Dried mucus in the eye's inner corner, perhaps left from sleep (sleepy sand).

quote.citation: 2018 January 3, Moran Eye Center, “Is That Morning 'Eye Gunk' Normal?”, in HealthFeed Blog‎[3], University of Utah Hospital, archived from the original on January 2, 2020:
quote.text: Sleep in your eyes, sleep crust, sand, eye gunk—whatever you call it, we all get it—that crusty stuff in the corners of your eyes when you wake up in the morning. "The medical term is 'rheum,' though you rarely hear it used,"  […]

definitions.definition: Of a light beige colour, like that of typical sand.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English sanden, from the noun (see above).

definitions.definition: (transitive) To abrade the surface of (something) with sand or sandpaper in order to smooth or clean it.

quote.citation: 1938, Xavier Herbert, chapter IX, in Capricornia‎[4], New York: D. Appleton-Century, published 1943, page 141:
quote.text: Sudden stopping, which could be effected easily by sanding the rails and reversing the driving-gear, was dangerous, because the train might telescope and overwhelm the engine.

quote.citation: 1958, Boris Pasternak, chapter 4, in Max Hayward, Manya Harari, transl., Doctor Zhivago, New York: Pantheon, page 96:
quote.text: The golden domes of churches and the freshly sanded paths in the town gardens were a glaring yellow.

definitions.definition: (transitive, historical) To blot ink using sand.

quote.citation: 1859, Charles Dickens, A Tale of Two Cities:
quote.text: The officer wrote until he had finished, read over to himself what he had written, sanded it, and handed it to Defarge, with the words "In secret."
